title: The lost art of the weekend
text: For an increasing number of professionals, the weekend has stopped being a break. A recent survey {{1}} that almost half of employees check work messages before breakfast on Saturdays, and a third admit to attending {{2}} calls from holiday beaches. The causes are familiar: smartphones that make us permanently {{3}}, workplaces that praise availability, and workloads that quietly expand. What is less familiar is the cost. Doctors link overwork to poor sleep, weakened immunity and {{4}} relationships; economists find that long hours beyond a certain point produce no extra output at all. Some countries have experimented with legal limits on out-of-hours contact, with {{5}} results: in France, employees have had a 'right to disconnect' since 2017. Companies, meanwhile, discover that rested employees are more, not less, {{6}}. Protecting the weekend, researchers insist, is not laziness but {{7}} for sustainable work — and it works best when it is {{8}} from the top.

gaps.explanation: 'a survey found that…' — the standard verb for research results.
'maintenance for sustainable work' — keeping it in good condition (noun).
'modelled from the top' = demonstrated by leaders' behaviour.
